Recovery after a **periacetabular osteotomy (PAO)** is usually measured in **months, not weeks**.

Typical timeline:
- **Hospital stay:** about **2–4 days** at HSS. ([hss.edu](https://www.hss.edu/health-library/conditions-and-treatments/pao-periacetabular-osteotomy?utm_source=openai))
- **Crutches / limited weight-bearing:** usually **6–8 weeks**. ([hss.edu](https://www.hss.edu/health-library/conditions-and-treatments/pao-periacetabular-osteotomy?utm_source=openai))
- **Return to school or desk-type work:** often around **3 months**. ([hss.edu](https://www.hss.edu/health-library/conditions-and-treatments/pao-periacetabular-osteotomy?utm_source=openai))
- **Return to regular activities:** commonly **3–6 months**, depending on healing and rehab progress. ([myhssmedia.hss.edu](https://myhssmedia.hss.edu/health-library/conditions-and-treatments/hip-dysplasia-adolescents-young-adults?utm_source=openai))
- **Return to sports:** often **6–12 months**. ([hss.edu](https://www.hss.edu/health-library/conditions-and-treatments/pao-periacetabular-osteotomy?utm_source=openai))

A simple way to think about it:
- **First 6–8 weeks:** protect the bone, use crutches, start PT.
- **By ~3 months:** many people are functioning much better day to day.
- **By 6–12 months:** fuller recovery, especially for athletics.

Recovery can be longer or shorter depending on:
- your age
- whether one or both hips are involved
- bone healing on X-rays
- muscle strength
- whether you also had other hip procedures done

Most people feel mostly recovered from a periacetabular osteotomy (PAO) in about **4 to 6 months**. Feeling fully back to normal often takes **9 to 12 months**, and some people keep improving for up to two years. A typical timeline looks like this:

**In the hospital (about 1–4 days)**
- Most people stay 2 to 4 days, but some hospitals send people home after 1–2 days.
- You will start physical therapy the day after surgery. Usually, they are able to sit in a chair a day after the procedure, and within one to two days after the surgery, they typically begin to walk with crutches.
- Plan on having someone to take care of you 24/7 for the first week.

**Weeks 0–8: Crutches**
- Crutches must be used for 6 to 8 weeks. Weight-bearing rules vary by surgeon. Some allow partial weight on the leg, while others allow none for the first six to eight weeks after surgery.
- One center says that in the next six weeks, you switch to one cane or crutch as your provider instructs.

**Months 2–3: Back to daily life**
- By two to three months after the surgery, most patients can put their full weight on the affected hip and return to everyday activities.
- Most individuals return to school or work after three months
- Pain usually will most likely be gone within four months after the operation.

**Months 4–12: Rehab and sports**
- A guided physical therapy program that lasts four to six months will be recommended to help people regain strength and range of motion in the hip.
- Most people can resume athletics between 6 to 12 months. One surgeon lets patients start swimming and cycling at four weeks and jogging at three months, but this varies a lot between surgeons.
- University of Utah Health says it usually takes 9–12 months to feel fully recovered, and that you will see continued improvements in your mobility and strength for up to two years after surgery.

Full recovery from rotator cuff surgery usually takes **about 4 to 12 months**. Where you land in that range depends mostly on how big the tear was. According to HSS, full recovery ranges from four months for small tears to up to 12 months for massive tears.

**Typical timeline:**
- **Weeks 0–6 (protecting the repair):** You wear a sling and only do passive motion, meaning someone else moves the arm for you. Pain and swelling are worst in this stage. The tendon has to heal back onto the bone, and that takes several weeks before it can take any real load. If you push it too early, the repair can fail.
- **Weeks 6–12 (active motion):** You start moving the shoulder with its own muscles and stop using the sling when your surgeon says so.
- **Months 3–5 (strengthening):** Resistance exercises are added slowly to rebuild the muscles that were protected for months.
- **Months 6–12 (full function):** You regain full strength and return to demanding activities. Larger tears take longer to get here.

**Key milestones:**
- **Desk work:** You may be able to return to a desk job with no lifting within 1–2 weeks.
- **Physical jobs:** Work that involves overhead reaching, repeated arm use, or lifting usually needs 3–6 months before full duty.
- **Driving:** Usually possible around 4–6 weeks after surgery.
- **Everyday activities:** Most people can do daily tasks comfortably within 4–6 months, though complete healing takes 9–12 months. Athletes in overhead sports may need 9–12 months.

**What can make recovery longer:** Larger tears or poor tendon quality. It can also take longer if you smoke, are over 65, or don't follow the rehab plan. Most patients go to physical therapy for about 4–6 months. Your surgeon will set the pace for your specific repair.
